claim: VEST (Voting and Election Science Team) edits at least one precinct boundary (splitting, merging, or redrawing) in roughly one-sixth of all US geographic units (mostly counties) in every general election cycle, demonstrating that precinct boundary churn between election cycles is a structural, recurring feature of election administration rather than a rare exception.
stance_target: bureau-de-vote boundary instability between election cycles (e.g. France 2022 to 2027) is a general phenomenon requiring systematic crosswalk methodology, not an edge case
quoted_support: In a given election, we edit at least one precinct -- and often more -- in about one-sixth of the geographical units. These are the geographic units where we make changes.
numbers: ~1/6 of geographic units edited per cycle

claim: VEST disaggregates 'at-large' vote totals (covering an entire county, state, or mail/early/provisional-ballot subcategory) to geographically-bound precincts using proportional allocation based on each candidate's existing vote share within the surrounding bound precincts, with a largest-remainder rounding rule to preserve exact county-level totals as whole numbers.
stance_target: concrete precedent algorithm for disaggregating non-geographic vote categories (e.g. postal/proxy/expatriate votes) into a geographically bounded precinct/bureau-de-vote panel
scope_conditions: United States precinct-level election reporting; general proration technique
quoted_support: Typically, we apportion a candidate's at-large votes to geographically-bound precincts proportional to the candidate's votes within the geographically-bound precincts. For example, if Joe Biden receives 100 votes in an at-large precinct and two geographically-bound precincts within it have 600 and 400 votes for Biden, we apportion 60 of the at-large Biden votes to the first precinct and 40 to the second.
numbers: example: 100 at-large votes split 60/40 by existing 600/400 vote ratio

claim: VEST's precinct database methodologically diverges from the competing MIT Election Data and Science Lab (MEDSL) database specifically on how at-large/reporting-unit votes are handled: VEST disaggregates them into geographically-bound precincts (geography-first) while MEDSL reports them as separate at-large rows (reporting-unit-first) -- because VEST's downstream use case (ecological inference, redistricting) requires precisely geolocated votes.
stance_target: there is no single canonical way to build a precinct-level election panel -- design choices depend on downstream analytical use case (geographic precision vs. faithful reporting-unit fidelity)
scope_conditions: United States, comparison of VEST vs. MIT Election Data and Science Lab precinct databases
quoted_support: An important distinction between our database and other precinct databases, such as the database produced by the MIT Election Data and Science Lab, is that these other data providers report at-large precincts as separate rows and do not disaggregate to geographically-bound precincts as we do.
entities: MIT Election Data and Science Lab

claim: VEST precinct-level databases have been used as evidentiary input in US Supreme Court redistricting litigation, including the successful racial-gerrymander challenge to Alabama's congressional districts, Allen v. Milligan, 599 U.S. 1 (2023), where experts used ecological inference on VEST precinct data to estimate racial voting patterns.
stance_target: harmonized precinct-level election panels are a load-bearing input for ecological-inference-based legal and advocacy analysis, not just academic exercises
scope_conditions: United States, Alabama congressional redistricting, decided 2023
quoted_support: A related use case is voting rights litigation, where experts analyze precinct data to estimate racial voting patterns using a technique known as ecological inference. Among the court cases using our databases was a successful challenge to Alabama's congressional districts as a racial gerrymander decided by the U.S. Supreme Court in Allen v. Milligan 599 U.S. 1 (2023).

claim: No standardized national format exists for US precinct boundary data: local election officials provide GIS shapefiles, map images (including hand-drawn maps and cell-phone photos), or written/verbal street-range descriptions, requiring VEST to manually reconstruct boundaries from ~3,000 local election offices for each election cycle.
stance_target: manual, labor-intensive precinct-boundary reconciliation is inherent to any decentralized election-administration system, not specific to France or the US
quoted_support: There is no standard format for precinct boundary data. ... The third-most frequent map format election officials provide us with is a written or verbal description. We encounter this situation in rural counties or small townships that have few precincts and little GIS capacity.
